blocks.text: "Works on my machine" happens when the code is the same but the environment isn't: different runtime versions, system libraries, OS packages, configuration or hardware architecture between developer, CI and production.

rows: glibc, OpenSSL, libpq versions differ; native wheels break
App A needs lib v1, app B needs v2 (dependency hell)
A tool installed by hand on a dev laptop, missing in prod
Env vars, file paths, locale, time zone
macOS case-insensitive FS vs Linux; CRLF vs LF

items: Language-level isolation (virtualenv, nvm, rbenv): isolates packages, not system libraries.
Lockfiles: pin app dependencies, not the OS.
Static binaries: work for Go-style apps, not Python/ML stacks with native extensions.

blocks.text: The image freezes the whole userland (runtime, system libs, packages, app) into one immutable artifact. It still shares the host kernel, and config must still be injected per environment.

Q: "What does 'works on my machine' actually mean technically, and how do containers fix it?" A: "The code is identical but the environment differs: runtime versions, system libraries, undeclared tools, config or CPU architecture. Containers package the full userland into an immutable image, so dev, CI and prod run the same bytes; only config and the kernel come from outside."

items: It's an environment problem, not a code problem.
System libraries and undeclared deps are the usual culprits.
virtualenv/lockfiles don't cover the OS layer.
Images freeze userland; kernel and config stay external.
